notes.b: Landforms are shaped by forces that build up the land and by forces that wear it down. The landscape you see reflects the balance between the two.
points: Endogenetic (endogenic) forces come from within the earth and raise the land, for example through crustal uplift (the rising of the earth's outer rocky layer, the crust).

Exogenetic (exogenic) forces act at the surface: weathering (breakdown of rock in place), erosion (wearing away and carrying off of material) and deposition (dropping of material) wear the land down and move material.
All landforms represent a balance between endogenetic and exogenetic forces, and this balance may change through time, so a landscape can shift as one force gains on the other.
notes.tip: A true/false question can ask about endogenic forces: they are internal forces from within the earth.

notes.b: The crust is not fixed in height. It sits on the layer beneath it and settles to a level that depends on the weight it carries, and isostasy is the name for that balance.
points: Isostasy is the state of balance between the crust and the denser mantle (the thick layer of hot rock under the crust) beneath it.
The crust floats on the mantle, as a block of wood floats in water. The mantle beneath the crust is called the asthenosphere.
Isostatic change is the adjustment of the crust's height that restores this balance when the load on the crust changes, so adding weight lowers the crust and removing weight lets it rise.

notes.b: Ice sheets add a heavy load to the crust, and melting removes it. The crust responds slowly in both directions.
points: Isostatic depression: the weight of an ice sheet presses the crust down into the mantle, as a heavy load pushes a floating block lower in water.
Isostatic rebound (also called recovery or uplift): when the ice melts and the load is removed, the crust slowly rises.
Rebound lags far behind melting, because the crust adjusts slowly, so land can still be rising long after the ice has gone.
Rebound is still continuing in some places: Scandinavia around the Gulf of Bothnia, Hudson Bay in Canada, and Scotland.

notes.b: Ice is not the only thing that changes the load on the crust. Surface processes do it too, by moving material from one place to another.
points: Denudation (the wearing away and lowering of the land surface by weathering and erosion) removes material from the land. Removing weight through erosion causes the crust to rise.
Heavy deposition adds weight to the crust, so it sinks; a delta (a landform built where a river drops its load at the sea) is one place where a large load builds up.

notes.b: The land and the sea can each change height, and the two must not be confused. Isostatic change moves the land. Eustatic change moves the sea.
points: Isostatic change is a local change in the height of the land relative to the sea.
Eustatic change is a worldwide change in sea level.
During glaciation, water locked up in ice sheets lowered sea level worldwide, because less water was left in the oceans.
When the ice melted, the meltwater returned to the oceans and raised sea level again.
The level of the land relative to the sea is the combined result of isostatic and eustatic change, so the coast can rise or sink depending on which effect is stronger.
notes.tip: Isostatic change means the land moves; eustatic change means the sea moves. Never swap them.

notes.h: Base level and landscapes out of balance
notes.b: Base level is the lowest level to which a river can erode, normally sea level. A relative change between land and sea alters it.
points: A river cannot erode its channel below base level, so sea level controls the lower course of every river.
Uplift faster than denudation: the land rises but is not worn down quickly enough to match, so features are left high above the present sea.
Sea level rising faster than the land: the sea reaches features that were cut when it stood lower.
Such landscapes show features that do not match present conditions, because the balance between endogenetic and exogenetic forces is temporarily out of balance.

notes.b: Where the land rises relative to sea level, the coast is emergent (rising out of the sea) and former shore features stand above the present tide reach.
points: Isostatic uplift lifts a former beach, its cliffs and its rock platform above present high tide, which is how a raised beach forms.
An old cliff line marks the position of the former sea cliffs, now inland of the sea.
A wave-cut notch is cut into the old cliff at the former sea level, where waves once undercut the rock.
Sea caves and stacks (pillars of rock left standing when waves cut away the land around them) stand above the present tide reach.
Beach shingle (rounded pebbles) lies on the raised beach.
A flat former wave-cut platform is a level rock shelf cut by waves at the former sea level.
Examples: raised beaches at Malin Head, Inishowen, Co. Donegal, and on the Isle of Jura, Scotland.
notes.tip: If asked for two coastal features formed by isostatic adjustment in an uplifted area, give raised beaches and related features such as the old cliff line or wave-cut platform.

notes.h: Rias, fjords and drowned drumlins (submergent coast)
notes.b: Where the sea stands higher relative to the land, the coast is submergent (sinking under the sea) and valleys and lowlands are flooded.
points: A ria is a drowned river valley. It has a V-shaped cross-section and a winding outline, because it was cut by a river.
Examples of rias: Bantry Bay, the Kenmare River and Dingle Bay (Co. Cork and Co. Kerry), and Cork Harbour. They are drowned river valleys of the Munster ridge-and-valley landscape.
A fjord is a drowned glacial trough (a valley deepened by a glacier). It is deep and U-shaped, often with a shallow threshold (a raised rock lip) at its mouth.
Examples of fjords: Killary Harbour, on the Co. Galway and Co. Mayo border, and the Norwegian fjords.
Drowned drumlins: a drumlin is an oval hill of glacial deposit, and when the lowland between drumlins floods, the crests of the drumlins stand as islands in the sea.
Examples of drowned drumlins: Clew Bay, Co. Mayo, and Strangford Lough, Co. Down.
notes.tip: Keep rias and fjords separate: a ria is a drowned river valley (V-shaped, winding), a fjord a drowned glacial valley (U-shaped, deep). For a submerged area, name rias, fjords and drowned drumlins.

notes.b: Ireland shows both kinds of coast, because the amount of ice, and so the amount of rebound, differed from north to south.
points: The north of Ireland had thicker ice, so it was depressed more and has undergone more isostatic rebound. Its coast shows raised beaches, as at Malin Head in Co. Donegal.
The south-west has the opposite pattern: its coast is drowned, with rias and related submerged features, as in Cork and Kerry.

notes.h: Rejuvenation after a fall in base level
notes.b: A fall in base level, caused by the land rising relative to the sea, gives a river renewed erosive power. This renewal is called rejuvenation.
points: The river erodes downwards again to the new, lower base level, and the renewed erosion works upstream from the mouth.
Knickpoint: a sudden steepening in the long profile (the line of the river's slope from source to mouth) of the river, which can form a waterfall.
Incised meanders: the river cuts down into its old meanders (bends), leaving them entrenched (cut deep) in steep-sided valleys.
River terraces: the old valley floor is left as a step above the new, lowered channel.
notes.tip: If asked for the name of the process that renews erosion in a river's old stage, the answer is rejuvenation.

notes.h: Drowned lower courses after a rise in base level
notes.b: The opposite change drowns rivers instead of renewing them. When the sea rises relative to the land, base level rises too.
points: A rise in base level, caused by the sea rising relative to the land, drowns the lower course of a river.
The drowned lower course becomes an estuary (the wide tidal mouth of a river) or a ria, a drowned river valley with a V-shaped cross-section and a winding outline.

keyTerms.definition: Forces from within the earth, such as crustal uplift, that raise or build up the land.
Surface processes of weathering, erosion and deposition that wear the land down and move material.
The state of balance between the crust, which floats on the denser mantle, and the mantle beneath it.
The downward sinking of the crust under the weight of an ice sheet.
The slow rise of the crust after an ice sheet melts and its load is removed.
A worldwide change in sea level, such as the lowering caused by water locked up in ice sheets.
The lowest level to which a river can erode, normally sea level.
Renewed erosive power in a river caused by a fall in base level.
A former beach, with its cliffs and platform, lifted above present high tide by isostatic uplift.
A coast where the land has risen relative to sea level.
A coast where the sea stands higher relative to the land, so valleys and lowlands are flooded.
A drowned river valley, V-shaped in cross-section and winding, flooded by a rise in sea level.
A drowned glacial trough, deep and U-shaped, often with a shallow threshold at its mouth.
A drumlin partly submerged by the sea, with its crest standing as an island.
A sudden steepening in a river's long profile, which marks the upstream limit of rejuvenated erosion.
A meander that the river has cut down into, leaving it entrenched in a steep-sided valley.
A step on a valley side marking an old valley floor, left above the present channel after rejuvenation.

factCards.term: Isostatic vs eustatic change: what is the difference?
factCards.definition: Isostatic change: the land moves, a local change in its height relative to the sea, e.g. rebound after an ice sheet melts. Eustatic change: the sea moves, a worldwide change in sea level, e.g. falling as water is locked in ice sheets and rising as it melts.

factCards.term: Isostatic rebound: why it continues today, and three places where it does
factCards.definition: Rebound lags far behind melting, so land can still be rising long after the ice has gone. It continues in Scandinavia around the Gulf of Bothnia, around Hudson Bay in Canada, and in Scotland.

factCards.term: Denudation and deposition: how they change the load on the crust
factCards.definition: Erosion removes weight from the land, so the crust rises. Heavy deposition adds weight, so the crust sinks; a delta is one place where a large load builds up.

factCards.term: Landscapes temporarily out of balance: the two situations
factCards.definition: Where uplift is faster than denudation, features such as raised beaches are left above the present sea. Where sea level rises faster than the land, the sea floods valleys cut when it stood lower, forming rias, fjords and drowned drumlins. Either way the features don't match present conditions.

factCards.term: Raised beaches: five features found on them, and two examples
factCards.definition: An old cliff line inland of the sea; a wave-cut notch at the former sea level; sea caves and stacks above the present tide reach; beach shingle; a flat former wave-cut platform. Examples: Malin Head, Inishowen, Co. Donegal; the Isle of Jura, Scotland.

factCards.term: Submergent coast: three features, with an example of each
factCards.definition: Rias (drowned river valleys), e.g. Bantry Bay; fjords (drowned glacial troughs), e.g. Killary Harbour on the Co. Galway–Co. Mayo border; drowned drumlins, e.g. Clew Bay, Co. Mayo, and Strangford Lough, Co. Down.

factCards.term: Name four rias in the south-west and the landscape they drowned
factCards.definition: Bantry Bay, the Kenmare River, Dingle Bay and Cork Harbour are drowned river valleys of the Munster ridge-and-valley landscape, flooded as the sea rose relative to the land.

factCards.term: North vs south-west of Ireland: how isostasy shaped each coast
factCards.definition: The north had thicker ice, so it was depressed more and has rebounded more: its coast shows raised beaches, as in Donegal. The south-west shows the opposite pattern: a drowned coast with rias, as in Cork and Kerry.

factCards.term: Fall in base level: effect on a river, and three landforms it leaves
factCards.definition: The land rises relative to the sea, giving the river renewed erosive power (rejuvenation); it cuts down again, working upstream from the mouth. Landforms: a knickpoint (often with a waterfall), incised meanders and river terraces.

factCards.term: Rise in base level: effect on a river's lower course
factCards.definition: When the sea rises relative to the land, the lower course of the river is drowned and becomes an estuary or a ria.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how isostasy impacts on the coastal landscape.
questions.model: The crust floats on the denser mantle. During glaciation the weight of the ice sheet depressed the crust, and when the ice melted the crust began to rise again by isostatic rebound. Rebound lags behind melting, so the land is still rising in places. Where the land rises relative to sea level the coast is emergent, and former shore features are left above the present tide reach. A raised beach has an old cliff line marking the former sea cliffs, and a wave-cut notch cut into the old cliff at the former sea level. Sea caves and stacks stand above the present tide reach, and beach shingle lies on a flat former wave-cut platform. Examples are the raised beaches at Malin Head, Inishowen, Co. Donegal, and on the Isle of Jura, Scotland. Where the sea stands higher relative to the land the coast is submergent and valleys are flooded. A ria is a drowned river valley, V-shaped in cross-section and winding, with examples at Bantry Bay, the Kenmare River and Dingle Bay, and Cork Harbour. A fjord is a drowned glacial trough, deep and U-shaped with a shallow threshold at its mouth, with examples at Killary Harbour and the Norwegian fjords. Drowned drumlins form where the lowland between drumlins floods and the drumlin crests stand as islands, with examples at Clew Bay, Co. Mayo, and Strangford Lough, Co. Down. The north of Ireland, with thicker ice and more rebound, has raised beaches, while the south-west has drowned coastlines.

questions.prompt: Explain how isostatic change can affect a river's landscape.
questions.model: Isostatic change alters the height of the land relative to the sea, and this changes base level. Where the land rises relative to the sea, base level falls. A fall in base level, caused by the land rising relative to the sea, gives a river renewed erosive power, which is called rejuvenation. The river erodes downwards again, and the renewed erosion works upstream from the mouth. Rejuvenation produces a knickpoint, a sudden steepening in the long profile that can form a waterfall. It also produces incised meanders, where the river has cut down into its old meanders and left them entrenched in steep-sided valleys, and river terraces, which are steps on the valley side marking the old valley floor above the new channel. A rise in base level, caused by the sea rising relative to the land, drowns the lower course of a river, which becomes an estuary or a ria.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between isostatic and eustatic change.
questions.model: Isostatic change is a change in the height of the land, as the crust rises or sinks in response to a change in its load. Eustatic change is a worldwide change in sea level, such as the lowering caused by water locked up in ice sheets.
